::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- clean text with `str_trim()`, `str_squish()`, `str_to_lower()`, `str_to_title()`, `str_replace()` and `str_sub()`;
- detect and extract patterns with `str_detect()` and `str_split()`, using five basic **regular expression** patterns;
- build text from data with `str_glue()`;
- fix inconsistent categories with `forcats` (`fct_recode()`, `fct_collapse()`, `fct_lump_n()`, `fct_infreq()`);
- parse dates with `ymd()` / `dmy()`, extract year, month and weekday, compute differences and round dates with `floor_date()`.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


## 1. Why clean strings and dates?

Data typed by people are messy. The same city appears as `"Rome"`, `"rome"` and `"Rome "` (with a trailing space). Prices are stored as text like `"€12.50"`. Dates arrive as `"05/03/2024"` — is that 5 March or 3 May?

For R, `"Rome"` and `"Rome "` are **different values**: a frequency table will count them separately, a [join](11-joins.qmd) will fail to match them, and a model will treat them as different categories. Cleaning text and dates is therefore not cosmetic: it decides **which units are counted together**, and so it changes the statistics.

All stringr functions start with `str_`, take the string(s) as the first argument and are vectorised: they work on a whole column at once.

## 2. Cleaning text with stringr


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c("  Rome", "rome ", "ROME", "Milan  centre")

str_trim(x)          # remove spaces at both ends
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Rome"          "rome"          "ROME"          "Milan  centre"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_squish(x)        # also collapse internal repeated spaces
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Rome"         "rome"         "ROME"         "Milan centre"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_to_lower(x)      # lower case
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "  rome"        "rome "         "rome"          "milan  centre"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_to_title(str_squish(x))   # Title Case
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Rome"         "Rome"         "Rome"         "Milan Centre"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_length(x)        # number of characters (spaces count!)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  6  5  4 13
```


:::
:::


`str_length()` shows why `"  Rome"` and `"Rome"` do not match: they have a different number of characters.

### Replacing and extracting parts


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
prices <- c("€12.50", "€7.00", "€30.10")

str_replace(prices, "€", "")            # replace the first match
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "12.50" "7.00"  "30.10"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_remove(prices, "€") |> as.numeric() # shortcut + convert to number
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 12.5  7.0 30.1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
codes <- c("IT-2024-001", "FR-2023-017", "ES-2024-112")
str_sub(codes, 1, 2)     # characters 1 to 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "IT" "FR" "ES"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_sub(codes, -3)       # the last three characters
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "001" "017" "112"
```


:::
:::


`str_replace()` changes only the **first** match in each string; `str_replace_all()` changes all of them. Negative positions in `str_sub()` count from the end.

### Splitting and combining


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
str_split("Adelie,Chinstrap,Gentoo", ",")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "Adelie"    "Chinstrap" "Gentoo"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_split_i(codes, "-", 2)     # the 2nd piece of each string
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024" "2023" "2024"
```


:::
:::


`str_split()` returns a **list** (each string can produce a different number of pieces); `str_split_i()` returns just the *i*-th piece as a vector. For splitting a column into several columns of a data frame use `separate_wider_delim()` from [Tidy data and reshaping](12-tidy-reshape.qmd).

`str_glue()` builds text by inserting values inside `{ }`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(m = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species) |>
  mutate(label = str_glue("{species}: {round(m)} g"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     species    m             label
#> 1    Adelie 3701    Adelie: 3701 g
#> 2    Gentoo 5076    Gentoo: 5076 g
#> 3 Chinstrap 3733 Chinstrap: 3733 g
```


:::
:::


This is handy for plot labels and automated reports.

## 3. A first look at regular expressions

`str_detect(string, pattern)` returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each string. The `pattern` is a **regular expression** (regex): a small language for describing text. Five patterns cover most everyday needs:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "kiwi 2", "Cherry", "pear.", "blueberry")
```
:::


| Pattern | Meaning | Matches in `fruits` |
|---|---|---|
| `"^b"` | starts with `b` | banana, blueberry |
| `"y$"` | ends with `y` | Cherry, blueberry |
| `"\\d"` | any digit | kiwi 2 |
| `"[aeiou]{2}"` | two vowels in a row | pear., blueberry |
| `"\\."` | a literal dot | pear. |


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
str_detect(fruits, "^b")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fruits[str_detect(fruits, "y$")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Cherry"    "blueberry"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_subset(fruits, "\\d")          # shortcut for x[str_detect(x, p)]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "kiwi 2"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_subset(fruits, "[aeiou]{2}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "pear."     "blueberry"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_subset(fruits, "\\.")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "pear."
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str_subset(fruits, "an|err")      # | means "or"
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "banana"    "Cherry"    "blueberry"
```


:::
:::


Two details you will need often:

- `.` means **any character**; to match a real dot write `"\\."` (the backslash "escapes" the special meaning, and in an R string it must itself be doubled).
- Matching is **case sensitive**: `"^c"` does not match `"Cherry"`. Lower-case the text first, or use `regex("^c", ignore_case = TRUE)`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
str_extract(c("kiwi 2", "pack of 12 eggs", "none"), "\\d+")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2"  "12" NA
```


:::
:::


`+` means "one or more of the previous", so `"\\d+"` extracts a whole number. Strings without a match give `NA`.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: a regex cheat sheet

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `.` | any character |
| `\\d`, `\\s`, `\\w` | digit, white space, "word" character (letter, digit, `_`) |
| `[abc]`, `[^abc]`, `[a-z]` | one of / none of / a range |
| `*`, `+`, `?`, `{n,m}` | 0 or more, 1 or more, 0 or 1, between n and m |
| `^`, `$` | start, end of the string |
| `(...)` | a group (used by `str_match()` and `names_pattern`) |

The vertical bar means "or": `"cat|dog"` matches either word.

stringr uses the ICU regex engine. The R4DS chapter "Regular expressions" is a gentle and complete introduction.
:::

## 4. Categorical variables: a forcats recap

Once a text column is clean, it is usually a categorical variable and should become a [factor](../01-foundations/06-factors.qmd). The forcats functions all start with `fct_`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
city <- c("Rome", "Milan", "Milano", "Roma", "Turin", "Rome", "Naples")

fct_recode(city, Milan = "Milano", Rome = "Roma") |> fct_count()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   f          n
#>   <fct>  <int>
#> 1 Milan      2
#> 2 Naples     1
#> 3 Rome       3
#> 4 Turin      1
```


:::
:::


`fct_recode(new = "old")` renames individual levels. To merge several levels into groups, use `fct_collapse()`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fct_collapse(city,
  North = c("Milan", "Milano", "Turin"),
  Centre = c("Rome", "Roma"),
  South = "Naples"
) |> fct_count()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   f          n
#>   <fct>  <int>
#> 1 North      3
#> 2 South      1
#> 3 Centre     3
```


:::
:::


Two functions are especially useful before tables and bar charts:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
models <- word(rownames(mtcars), 1)   # first word = brand
fct_infreq(models) |> levels() |> head()        # order levels by frequency
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Merc"   "Fiat"   "Hornet" "Mazda"  "Toyota" "AMC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fct_lump_n(models, n = 3) |> fct_count(sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   f          n
#>   <fct>  <int>
#> 1 Other     17
#> 2 Merc       7
#> 3 Fiat       2
#> 4 Hornet     2
#> 5 Mazda      2
#> 6 Toyota     2
```


:::
:::


`fct_infreq()` orders levels from most to least frequent; `fct_lump_n(n = 3)` keeps the three most frequent levels (plus ties) and merges the rest into `"Other"`. Missing values can be made an explicit level with `fct_na_value_to_level()`.

## 5. Dates with lubridate

### Parsing: from text to `Date`

Base R's `as.Date()` expects the ISO format `"YYYY-MM-DD"`. With other formats it can silently go wrong:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.Date("05/03/2024")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "0005-03-20"
```


:::
:::


R read this as the year 5! lubridate's parsing functions are named after the **order** of the components: `ymd()`, `dmy()`, `mdy()`, … They accept any common separator.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ymd("2024-03-05")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024-03-05"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
dmy(c("05/03/2024", "5-3-2024", "05.03.2024"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024-03-05" "2024-03-05" "2024-03-05"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mdy("March 5, 2024")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024-03-05"
```


:::
:::


Choose the function from how the data were *recorded*: European data are usually `dmy`, US data `mdy`. Strings that cannot be parsed become `NA`, with a warning.

### Extracting components


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
d <- ymd(c("2024-03-05", "2024-07-14", "2024-12-25"))

year(d)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 2024 2024 2024
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
month(d)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  3  7 12
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
month(d, label = TRUE)                  # an ordered factor
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] mar lug dic
#> 12 Levels: gen < feb < mar < apr < mag < giu < lug < ago < set < ... < dic
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
wday(d, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)   # weekday, weeks starting on Monday
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] mar dom mer
#> Levels: lun < mar < mer < gio < ven < sab < dom
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
yday(d)                                 # day of the year
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  65 196 360
```


:::
:::


`month(label = TRUE)` and `wday(label = TRUE)` return **ordered factors**, so tables and plots show months in calendar order rather than alphabetically.

### Differences and rounding


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
start <- ymd("2024-03-05")
end   <- ymd("2024-07-17")

end - start                         # a difftime, in days
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> Time difference of 134 days
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.numeric(end - start)             # just the number
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 134
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
time_length(interval(start, end), "months")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 4.387
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
start + days(30)                    # arithmetic with periods
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024-04-04"
```


:::
:::


`floor_date()` rounds dates **down** to a unit — the key tool for summarising by week or month:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
floor_date(d, "month")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024-03-01" "2024-07-01" "2024-12-01"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
floor_date(d, "week", week_start = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2024-03-04" "2024-07-08" "2024-12-23"
```


:::
:::


### Applied: building dates in `airquality`

`airquality` stores the date in two columns, `Month` and `Day`, of the year 1973. `make_date()` combines them:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
aq <- airquality |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(date = make_date(1973, Month, Day),
         weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1))

aq |>
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(Temp), n = n(), .by = weekday) |>
  arrange(weekday)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   weekday mean_temp     n
#>   <ord>       <dbl> <int>
#> 1 lun         77.90    21
#> 2 mar         79.14    22
#> 3 mer         77.23    22
#> 4 gio         78.59    22
#> 5 ven         77.18    22
#> 6 sab         77.64    22
#> 7 dom         77.5     22
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- Because `weekday` is an ordered factor, `arrange()` sorts it from Monday to Sunday.
- The mean temperatures are very similar across weekdays (between about 77 and 79 °F): no surprise, since the weather does not know which day of the week it is. A weekday effect would be expected for *traffic* pollution, not for temperature.
:::

## 6. Applied mini-example: cleaning a messy table

A small survey was typed in by hand:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
messy <- tibble(
  name   = c("  ada LOVELACE", "Ben  Smith ", "chiara ROSSI",
             "Dev patel", "eli  MARTIN"),
  city   = c("rome", "Rome ", "MILAN", "milano", "Rome"),
  phone  = c("+39 333 123 4567", "333-987-6543", "(333) 555 0000",
             "3331112222", NA),
  signup = c("05/03/2024", "5-4-2024", "17.06.2024", "01/08/2024",
             "30/09/2024"),
  spent  = c("€12.50", "€ 7", "30,00 €", "15.2", "€0")
)
messy
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   name             city     phone            signup     spent  
#>   <chr>            <chr>    <chr>            <chr>      <chr>  
#> 1 "  ada LOVELACE" "rome"   +39 333 123 4567 05/03/2024 €12.50 
#> 2 "Ben  Smith "    "Rome "  333-987-6543     5-4-2024   € 7    
#> 3 "chiara ROSSI"   "MILAN"  (333) 555 0000   17.06.2024 30,00 €
#> 4 "Dev patel"      "milano" 3331112222       01/08/2024 15.2   
#> 5 "eli  MARTIN"    "Rome"   <NA>             30/09/2024 €0
```


:::
:::


Every column has a problem: inconsistent case and spaces, two spellings of Milan, phone numbers in different formats, dates with different separators, amounts with currency symbols and a decimal comma. One pipeline fixes them all:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean <- messy |>
  mutate(
    name   = name |> str_squish() |> str_to_title(),
    city   = city |> str_trim() |> str_to_title() |>
      fct_recode(Milan = "Milano"),
    phone  = phone |> str_remove_all("[^0-9]") |> str_sub(-10),
    signup = dmy(signup),
    spent  = spent |> str_replace(",", ".") |>
      str_remove_all("[^0-9.]") |> as.numeric()
  )
clean
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   name         city  phone      signup     spent
#>   <chr>        <fct> <chr>      <date>     <dbl>
#> 1 Ada Lovelace Rome  3331234567 2024-03-05  12.5
#> 2 Ben Smith    Rome  3339876543 2024-04-05   7  
#> 3 Chiara Rossi Milan 3335550000 2024-06-17  30  
#> 4 Dev Patel    Milan 3331112222 2024-08-01  15.2
#> 5 Eli Martin   Rome  <NA>       2024-09-30   0
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- `name`: extra spaces removed and Title Case applied.
- `city`: a **factor** with 2 levels instead of 5 different spellings.
- `phone`: `"[^0-9]"` means "any character that is *not* a digit"; removing them and keeping the last 10 digits drops the country code `+39`. The missing phone stays `NA` — cleaning must not invent data.
- `signup`: a real `Date`, so we can compute with it.
- `spent`: a number, so we can summarise it.
:::

Now the data can be analysed:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean |>
  summarise(
    customers   = n(),
    total_spent = sum(spent),
    first_signup = min(signup),
    .by = city
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   city  customers total_spent first_signup
#>   <fct>     <int>       <dbl> <date>      
#> 1 Rome          3        19.5 2024-03-05  
#> 2 Milan         2        45.2 2024-06-17
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
clean |>
  mutate(signup_month = month(signup, label = TRUE)) |>
  count(signup_month)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   signup_month     n
#>   <ord>        <int>
#> 1 mar              1
#> 2 apr              1
#> 3 giu              1
#> 4 ago              1
#> 5 set              1
```


:::
:::


On the raw `messy` table, the first summary would have shown five "cities" and could not have computed a total.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Invisible spaces.** `"Rome "` ≠ `"Rome"`. Use `str_trim()`/`str_squish()` on every text column that will be grouped or joined.
2. **Forgetting to escape special characters** in regex: `"."` matches anything, `"\\."` matches a dot; `"$"` means "end of string", so to match a dollar sign write `"\\$"`.
3. **Parsing dates with the wrong order.** `"05/03/2024"` is 5 March with `dmy()` and 3 May with `mdy()`. Both "work"; only one is right. Check with a date whose day is above 12.
4. **`as.Date()` on non-ISO text** can silently produce absurd dates (year 5). Check `range()` of every new date column.
5. **Cleaning that invents information:** filling a missing phone or guessing an ambiguous date. Leave genuine unknowns as `NA`.
:::

## 7. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What does `str_detect(x, "^[A-Z]")` test?

Whether each string **starts with** an upper-case letter. `^` anchors the pattern at the start; `[A-Z]` is one character between A and Z.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Why is `month(d, label = TRUE)` better than `format(d, "%b")` for a frequency table?

`month(label = TRUE)` returns an **ordered factor**, so the table lists months in calendar order (Jan, Feb, …). `format()` returns plain text, which is sorted alphabetically (Apr, Aug, Dec, …).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. A column has the values "M", "m", "male", "F", "female", "Female". How would you obtain a clean factor with two levels?

Lower-case the text with `str_to_lower()`, then `fct_collapse(x, male = c("m", "male"), female = c("f", "female"))`.
:::

### Interactive (run in your browser)


`make_date(1973, Month, Day)` and the unit `"week"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_13_4"}
```r
airquality |>
  mutate(date = make_date(1973, Month, Day),
         week = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)) |>
  summarise(mean_ozone = mean(Ozone, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_obs = sum(!is.na(Ozone)),
            .by = week) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_ozone))
```
The top of the list is the week starting 25 June 1973 — but look at `n_obs`: its mean is based on a **single day**, because most June ozone values are missing. Among weeks with at least five observations, the highest means are in August (weeks starting 27 and 6 August). A mean based on one value is not a reliable summary of a week; always report `n` next to it.

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — your own messy table.** Create a tibble with 6 rows and the columns `sex` (values like `"M"`, `" f"`, `"Female"`, `"male "`), `birth` (dates written as `"1999-03-12"`, `"2001/11/05"`, …) and `height` (text like `"1,72 m"`, `"1.80m"`). Clean it so that `sex` is a factor with two levels, `birth` is a `Date`, `height` is numeric in centimetres, and add the age in whole years on 1 January 2025.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
people <- tibble(
  sex    = c("M", " f", "Female", "male ", "F", "m"),
  birth  = c("1999-03-12", "2001/11/05", "2000-01-30",
             "1998.07.21", "2002-12-01", "1997/05/17"),
  height = c("1,72 m", "1.80m", "1,65 m", "1.91 m", "1.58m", "1,77m")
)

people |>
  mutate(
    sex = sex |> str_trim() |> str_to_lower() |>
      fct_collapse(male = c("m", "male"), female = c("f", "female")),
    birth  = ymd(birth),
    height = height |> str_replace(",", ".") |>
      str_remove_all("[^0-9.]") |> as.numeric() * 100,
    age = floor(time_length(interval(birth, ymd("2025-01-01")), "years"))
  )
```
Check the result with `glimpse()`: `sex` should be `<fct>`, `birth` `<date>`, `height` and `age` `<dbl>`.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Task | Function(s) |
|---|---|
| Remove spaces | `str_trim()`, `str_squish()` |
| Change case | `str_to_lower()`, `str_to_upper()`, `str_to_title()` |
| Find patterns | `str_detect()`, `str_subset()`, `str_extract()` |
| Replace / remove | `str_replace()`, `str_replace_all()`, `str_remove_all()` |
| Pieces of strings | `str_sub()`, `str_split()`, `str_split_i()` |
| Build text | `str_glue()` |
| Fix categories | `fct_recode()`, `fct_collapse()`, `fct_lump_n()`, `fct_infreq()` |
| Parse dates | `ymd()`, `dmy()`, `mdy()`, `make_date()` |
| Date parts | `year()`, `month(label = TRUE)`, `wday(label = TRUE)`, `yday()` |
| Date arithmetic | `d2 - d1`, `time_length(interval(d1, d2), "years")`, `days()`, `floor_date()` |

- Text values that look the same may not be equal: trim, squish and fix the case before grouping or joining.
- Five regex patterns (`^`, `$`, `\\d`, `[...]`, `|`) cover most cleaning tasks; escape special characters with `\\`.
- Parse dates with the function that matches the order in which they were recorded, then check their range.
- Cleaning decides which units are counted together: do it explicitly, in code, and never invent values.
